title: The same word
hookLine: two verses sharing a word may share a law

cards: Two people who've never met mention the same small town, and suddenly they're talking like cousins. A shared word can build a bridge between two places that seemed to have nothing in common.
The rabbis noticed the Torah can do it too. A verse about a burial plot bought from a stranger and a verse about a man marrying a woman sit books apart. They share one ordinary verb.
And on that one verb, the Talmud builds a bridge strong enough to carry a law.

teach.b: Gezerah shavah. The rule that when two verses share a word, they may share a law: what's clear in one place can be carried to the other. Here's the bridge from the hook.

The Mishnah, at the opening of tractate Kiddushin, lists the ways a marriage can begin, and one of them is with money. The Gemara asks: how do we know money works? The answer is a gezerah shavah on the word take.
In Deuteronomy, the Torah speaks of a man who takes a wife.

teach.h: TAKE: A FIELD AND A MARRIAGE.
teach.b: In Genesis, Abraham is buying a cave to bury Sarah, and he tells Ephron, the owner of the field, that he'll give the money for it: take it from me. Take there, take here.
In Genesis, taking happens with money, so in Deuteronomy, taking a wife can happen with money too. Notice what it isn't. It isn't a pun.
The Talmud treats it as a rule with serious limits. The big one: a person may not make up a gezerah shavah on their own.
It has to come down from teachers who received it. Without that limit, anyone could link any two verses that share a common word, and make the Torah say almost anything.
So the bridge is real, but you walk the ones that were handed to you.
Under the rule sits a classical belief: that the Torah's words are chosen so carefully that the same word in two places can carry meaning across.

how: Talmud students learn each gezerah shavah as a link handed down by earlier teachers, tracing the shared word back to both verses rather than inventing new links of their own.

practice: Choose one word that matters to you, home, maybe, or rest, or enough, and find two places in your life where it lives: home in your body, home in a person. Hold both at once and let the word be the bridge between them.
Walk across slowly a few times, without forcing anything.
